item.title: When a release goes wrong: a five-step incident playbook
item.description: Detect, contain, communicate, fix and recover. A practical playbook for web app incidents, and the ACR feature that helps at each step.
item.content:encoded:
Every team that ships will eventually ship something broken. What separates a five-minute blip from a lost evening is rarely the bug itself. It is how quickly you notice, how much of the damage you can stop before the fix exists, and whether your users know what is going on.

This is a playbook for that moment. It has five steps, and at each one we point to the part of ACR built for it.

1. Detect: hear about it before your users tell you​

The worst way to learn about an incident is a support ticket. Set up signals that reach you first.

  • Alert rules. In Alerts, create rules for the things that really mean trouble: a new or regressed error issue, an error spike, p95 latency above a threshold, poor Web Vitals, a release whose crash-free sessions drop, or an app that stops sending data. Send them to email, Slack, Discord, Teams or a webhook. Cooldowns and mute windows keep a noisy rule from paging you every minute.
  • Uptime checks. Uptime checks your public URLs every 5 to 60 minutes and opens an incident after the number of consecutive failures you choose, then resolves it when checks recover.
  • Releases. If you set appVersion in your SDK, Releases shows adoption, crash-free sessions and newly introduced issues for each version. A bad release stands out in the comparison.

Tip: test every alert rule against your app's real traffic before you rely on it. A threshold that fires all the time gets muted; one that never fires is not protecting you.

2. Contain: stop the damage before the fix exists​

This is the step most teams skip, because without the right levers the only option is "deploy a fix". You have faster options, from smallest to largest blast radius:

Turn the feature off. If the broken code is behind a feature flag, switch the flag's Enabled off, or lower its rollout. Everyone receives the default value on the next poll.

Get users off the bad version. If the problem is in the browser bundle and you have already deployed a fix, open the release policy in Controls and set a minimum version. In force mode, tabs below it reload once onto the new code. Or send a one-shot reload command to every open tab.

Clear what is stuck. A bad service worker or a corrupted cache entry can keep serving broken assets after you fixed them. A clear cache command tells every browser running the app to drop Cache Storage, service workers, local storage, session storage, IndexedDB or script-readable cookies (you choose which), and optionally reload. Each browser applies it at most once, and the command history shows how many reachable browsers have applied it.

Close the doors. If the problem risks data, such as broken payments or writes that corrupt records, turn on maintenance mode. Browser SDKs cover the app with a full-page screen. Add your own user ids to the exemption list so your team can keep testing in production. On servers, the Express middleware and the NestJS guard answer 503 with Retry-After when you enable them, while health checks keep passing.

Quiet the noise. In the rare case that your own telemetry is part of the problem, such as a log loop flooding the network, lower the sample rate, raise the minimum log level, or use the collection kill switch.

Controls, announcements and commands need the admin role, because they affect every user at once. Decide in advance who on your team holds it, so you are not hunting for an admin mid-incident.

3. Communicate: tell people before they guess​

Silence makes every incident feel worse. A short message buys a lot of patience.

  • Announcement banner. Publish an announcement with severity warning or critical, a message such as "Payments are delayed. Your orders are safe, and we are working on it.", and optionally a link to a status page. Every visitor sees it on the next poll. Schedule an end time, or end it yourself when things are fixed.
  • Maintenance message. If you closed the doors, the maintenance screen is your message. Say what is happening and roughly when you expect to be back. The expected time is informational; maintenance never ends by itself.

4. Fix: from symptom to line​

Now that the damage is contained, you can fix the bug calmly instead of under fire.

  • Errors groups occurrences into one issue with a readable stack trace, the affected users and the versions it appeared in. If you upload source maps through CI, browser stack traces point to your original code instead of the minified bundle.
  • Logs let you filter by level, source, message or trace id around the time of the incident, and tail new lines live while you reproduce.
  • Performance shows whether a route became slower, at p50, p95 and p99, if the problem is speed rather than failure.

Ship the fix with a new appVersion, so you can see it take over in Releases.

5. Recover: reopen carefully, then learn​

Undo your containment in the reverse order you applied it, and watch as you go:

  1. Check the fix yourself first. If you used maintenance mode, your exempt user id lets you use the real app.
  2. Turn maintenance off, or bring the flag back to a small rollout instead of jumping straight to 100%.
  3. End the announcement, or replace it with a short "resolved" message.
  4. Watch Errors and Releases until the new version carries most sessions and the issue stops recurring.
  5. Resolve the alert incident.

Then write down what happened while it is fresh: how you noticed, how long containment took, and what would have made it faster. Usually the answer is one more flag around a risky change, or one more alert rule that would have fired sooner.

The playbook on one page​

StepGoalIn ACR
DetectKnow firstAlerts, Uptime, Releases
ContainStop the damageFlags, release policy, reload and clear cache, maintenance, kill switch
CommunicateKeep trustAnnouncements, maintenance message
FixFind the causeErrors, Logs, Performance, source maps
RecoverReopen safelyGradual rollout, Releases, resolving incidents

The best time to set this up is before you need it. Add an alert rule, wrap your next risky feature in a flag, and make sure someone on the team knows where the maintenance switch is. Read Remote controls for every lever in detail.

item.title: Ship behind a flag: gradual rollouts without a redeploy
item.description: How ACR feature flags work, why each user keeps the same result, and a step-by-step recipe for taking a feature from 0% to 100% safely.
item.content:encoded:
The safest deploy is one that changes nothing. Merge the new code, ship it switched off, and decide later, from a console, who gets to see it. If it misbehaves, switch it off again. No revert, no hotfix, no second deploy.

That is what feature flags are for. This post explains how flags work in ACR and walks through a rollout recipe you can use on your next feature.

Decouple deploying from releasing​

Without flags, deploying code and releasing a feature are the same event. Every deploy is a bet on everything inside it, and the only way to back out is another deploy.

With a flag, they come apart:

  • Deploy whenever the code is ready, with the feature off.
  • Release when you choose: to your team, then a small share of users, then everyone.
  • Roll back by changing a number in the console. The change reaches running apps on their next poll, about a minute later.

Creating a flag​

In the ACR console, open Flags and create one. The fields that matter most:

FieldWhat it does
KeyThe name your code reads, such as new-checkout. It cannot change later, so pick it carefully
Typeboolean, string, number or json
EnabledA disabled flag always returns the default, whatever else is configured
ValueWhat people inside the rollout or allow-list receive
Default valueWhat everyone else receives
RolloutThe percentage of users who receive the value, from 0 to 100
Always on for these usersUp to 100 user ids that always receive the value

Developers and above can create and edit flags; everyone on the app can read them.

Reading a flag in code​

Every ACR SDK can read flags. In React:

TSX
import { useFlag } from '@lib-acr/react';

export function Checkout() {
  const newCheckout = useFlag('new-checkout', false);
  return newCheckout ? <NewCheckout /> : <OldCheckout />;
}

In a plain browser app it is acr.flag('new-checkout', false). On a server, the Node.js SDK does not know who the request is for, so you pass the user:

TypeScript
const enabled = acr.flag('new-checkout', false, { userId: req.user?.id });

The second argument is the fallback your code uses when the flag does not exist yet, or before the first snapshot arrives.

Two properties make this cheap enough to use everywhere:

  • No network request per check. The SDK keeps the latest control snapshot in memory and evaluates flags locally. A flag check is a function call, not an API call.
  • It keeps working offline. If ACR is unreachable, the SDK uses the last values it saw. If it never saw any, your fallback wins.

Why each user keeps the same result​

A rollout is only useful if it is stable. If a user saw the new checkout on one page load and the old one on the next, your rollout would be a source of bugs, not a safety net.

ACR evaluates a flag in a fixed order:

  1. Missing or disabled → the default.
  2. The subject is your identified user id, or the visitor's anonymous id if you have not called identify().
  3. Subject in the allow-list → the value.
  4. Otherwise, a stable hash of the flag key and the subject gives a bucket from 0 to 99. A bucket below the rollout percentage receives the value; everyone else gets the default.

Because the bucket depends only on the flag key and the subject:

  • The same person always lands in the same bucket, on every device where you identify them, in the browser and on the server.
  • Raising the rollout only adds people. Going from 25% to 50% keeps everyone who already had the feature and adds the next 25 buckets. Nobody flips back and forth.
  • Lowering it removes people in the reverse order, which is exactly what you want when something looks wrong.

The rollout recipe​

Here is a sequence that works for most features.

1. Ship it dark. Create the flag with Enabled on, Rollout 0%, and your team's user ids in the allow-list. Deploy the code. Nobody outside your team sees anything.

2. Test in production. Use the real app, with real data and real traffic around you. This catches what staging never does: production config, third-party scripts, real browsers.

3. Open it to 5%. Watch Errors for new issues and Performance for slower routes. Give it long enough to see a normal day's traffic.

4. Step up: 25%, then 50%. Keep watching. If you run a release at the same time, compare its crash-free sessions against the previous version.

5. Go to 100%. Leave the flag in place for a while as a kill switch.

6. Clean up. Once you are confident, remove the flag check from the code and delete the flag. Flags that live forever become a second, invisible configuration system.

If anything goes wrong at any step: switch Enabled off. Every user gets the default on the next poll, about a minute later, and immediately when a browser tab comes back into focus.

Beyond on and off​

Boolean flags cover most rollouts, but ACR flags can do more:

  • Typed values. A number flag can tune a limit, a string flag can pick a copy variant, and a json flag can carry a small configuration object of up to 4 KB.
  • Targeting rules. Ordered conditions on user or visitor attributes decide who receives which value.
  • Weighted variants. Serve more than two named variants in fixed proportions.
  • Scheduled changes. Plan a rollout step, a value change or an enable for a specific time.
  • Experiments. Give a flag two or more variants, pick a conversion event such as purchase_completed, and Experiments compare conversion rates and tell you when the difference is statistically significant.

One rule: no secrets in flags​

Flag values are delivered to browsers. Anyone can read them in developer tools. Use flags to decide what to show, never to carry API keys, tokens or anything else you would not print on the page.

Try it on your next feature​

Pick the riskiest thing you are building this week, wrap it in useFlag or acr.flag, and ship it at 0%. The full reference is in Feature flags. If you have not connected an app yet, start with Connect your first app.

item.title: You vibe coded it in a weekend. Now run production the same way.
item.description: AI assistants made building an app fast and conversational. Running it in production is still slow and scary. ACR brings the same "describe it, see it, change it" feel to the part that comes after launch.
item.content:encoded:
Building software has never been faster. You describe a screen, an AI assistant writes it, you look at it in the browser, you ask for a change, and an hour later you have something that used to take a sprint. People call it vibe coding, and whatever you think of the name, the result is real: more apps reach production, built by smaller teams, sometimes by one person.

Then the app goes live, and the vibe stops.

The gap after launch​

Production asks questions that the build loop never did:

  • Is anyone actually using it? Which pages do they visit, and where do they drop off?
  • What is breaking right now, for whom, and since which version?
  • That new feature you generated on Tuesday: can you turn it off without regenerating and redeploying everything?
  • Users are stuck on an old bundle. How do you get them onto the new one?
  • You need to take the app down for ten minutes. Do you have a maintenance page? Does it reach people who already have the app open?

When you build fast, you also accumulate code you did not write line by line. That is fine while you are iterating in your editor. In production it means you need to see what that code is doing, and you need a way to change its behaviour faster than you can change the code.

Most teams answer this with a stack of tools, each with its own setup, its own dashboard and its own learning curve. For someone who just built an entire app in a weekend, that is a strange step backwards.

Run production like you built it​

The thing that makes vibe coding feel good is a tight loop: describe → see → adjust. ACR gives you the same loop for a running app.

See it: one install, instant signal​

Add one SDK and the app starts telling you what is happening. For a React app it is a provider around your root:

TSX
import { ACRProvider } from '@lib-acr/react';

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')!).render(
  <ACRProvider
    config={{
      apiKey: import.meta.env.VITE_ACR_API_KEY,
      endpoint: import.meta.env.VITE_ACR_ENDPOINT,
      appVersion: '1.0.0',
    }}
  >
    <App />
  </ACRProvider>,
);

That one change gives you visitors and sessions, page views, Core Web Vitals, and uncaught errors grouped into issues with stack traces. The ACR console has copy-ready snippets for React, Angular, plain browser apps, Node.js, Express and NestJS, so this is also an easy thing to hand to your assistant: "add the ACR SDK using this snippet" is a one-shot prompt.

When you want more, describe what matters in your own words and record it:

TSX
import { useACREvent } from '@lib-acr/react';

const track = useACREvent();
track('checkout_started', { cartSize: 3 });

Adjust it: switches instead of redeploys​

This is where ACR differs from a dashboard. Every change below happens from the console, reaches running apps in about a minute, and needs no new build:

You want to…In ACR
Hide a feature that is misbehavingTurn its feature flag off
Try a feature on yourself firstPut your user id in the flag's allow-list, rollout 0% for everyone else
Release it graduallyRaise the rollout: 5%, 25%, 50%, 100%
Take the app down brieflyTurn on maintenance mode, with your own id exempt
Tell users somethingPublish an announcement banner
Get everyone onto the new versionSet a release policy, or reload every open tab
Fix a broken service worker or cacheSend a clear-cache command to every browser

Wrapping new work in a flag is a one-line habit that pays off immediately:

TSX
import { useFlag } from '@lib-acr/react';

const newCheckout = useFlag('new-checkout', false);
return newCheckout ? <NewCheckout /> : <OldCheckout />;

The flag is evaluated inside the SDK, so this check is free and works offline. When you ask your assistant to build a risky feature, ask it to put the feature behind a flag too. Shipping switched off becomes your default, and "undo" stops meaning "regenerate and redeploy".

Guardrails you get for free​

Fast builders tend to skip the boring parts. ACR has sensible defaults for the ones that bite in production:

  • Keys that are safe in a browser. Browser apps use a publishable key that only works from the origins you allow. Server secrets are shown once, and the browser SDK refuses to run with one, so a secret cannot slip into a bundle unnoticed.
  • Privacy by default. Query strings are stripped, sensitive keys like passwords and tokens are redacted, email addresses in free text are masked, and visitor IP addresses are never stored.
  • Telemetry that cannot crash your app. SDK calls never throw, buffers have a fixed size, and if ACR is unreachable your app keeps working.
  • Roles when you add people. Invite a collaborator as a viewer or developer; only admins and owners can flip controls that affect every user.

A Monday morning, the ACR way​

Here is what running a small app looks like once this is in place:

  1. Open the app's Overview: connected, live visitors, nothing alarming.
  2. Glance at Errors: one new issue since last night's release, 14 users affected.
  3. Open it: the stack trace points at the new address form, behind the new-address-form flag.
  4. Set that flag's rollout back to 0%. Within a minute, nobody sees the broken form.
  5. Ask your assistant to fix the bug, paste in the stack trace, deploy when ready.
  6. Turn the flag back on for yourself, check it, then roll it out again.

No pager drama, no hotfix rush, no full redeploy just to hide a button. Building and running feel like the same activity again.

Get started​

Connect your first app takes a few minutes. If you want the bigger picture first, read Why web apps need a control room.

item.title: Why web apps need a control room
item.description: Dashboards tell you something is wrong. A control room lets you do something about it in the next minute, not after the next deploy.
item.content:encoded:
It is 9:40 on a Friday evening. Your error tracker lights up: the new checkout is throwing for a slice of users. You can see the stack trace. You can see the release it came from. You can even see which line is wrong.

And then you wait. For a fix to be written, reviewed, built, deployed and cached away. Twenty minutes if you are lucky, an hour if the pipeline is slow, longer if the person who knows that code is on a train.

Seeing a problem and being able to act on it are two different capabilities. Most web apps have the first and almost none of the second.

The deploy is the wrong lever for most incidents​

When the only way to change production is to ship code, every response to every problem goes through the slowest, riskiest step you have. A deploy:

  • takes minutes, and under pressure those minutes feel longer;
  • carries everything else that was merged since the last release, not just the fix;
  • can itself fail, which turns one incident into two;
  • does nothing for users who already have the old JavaScript loaded in an open tab.

That last point is easy to forget. A browser app keeps running whatever bundle it loaded until the tab reloads. Fix the server and the browser half of your users is still on yesterday's code, possibly for days.

Most of what you want to do in an incident is not "change the code". It is one of a handful of operational moves:

What you needWhat it looks like
Stop the bleedingTurn the broken feature off
Buy timeShow a maintenance page or a banner
Tell people"Payments are delayed, we are on it"
Get users off a bad versionAsk or force open tabs to reload
Undo a bad cacheClear service workers and storage in the browser
Quiet the noiseLower log volume or sample telemetry

None of those should need a build.

What a control room is​

Power plants, airports and broadcasters all have one: a room where the people responsible can see the state of the system and change it from the same desk. The screens and the switches are side by side, because the whole point is to close the loop between noticing and acting.

A web app deserves the same. In practice that means three things.

1. Signals you trust​

You cannot steer what you cannot see. That starts with the basics: errors grouped into issues instead of a firehose, logs you can tail and filter, request latency and Core Web Vitals, and whether each release is actually healthy. In ACR that is the Monitor side: Errors, Logs, Performance, Releases, Uptime and Alerts.

2. Levers that work in seconds​

Then you need switches that change behaviour without touching the code path you are worried about:

  • Feature flags to turn a feature off for everyone, or on for a few.
  • Maintenance mode that covers the app with a clear message while you fix things, with an exemption list so your team can test before reopening.
  • Announcements to put a banner in front of every visitor.
  • A release policy that prompts outdated tabs to update, or forces a reload below a minimum version.
  • One-shot commands to reload every open tab, or clear Cache Storage, service workers and local storage.
  • A telemetry kill switch and sampling, for the rare incident that your own logging is making worse.

In ACR these live on the Control side: Controls and Flags. Changes reach running apps in about a minute, immediately when a tab regains focus.

3. One place, one set of permissions​

When signals and levers live in different tools, you spend the first ten minutes of an incident logging in to things. You also end up with different people able to do different things in each tool, with nobody quite sure who can flip what.

In ACR both halves belong to the same app and the same membership. Viewers can read everything. Developers can manage keys and flags. Only admins and owners can change controls, because those affect every user at once. The role is the same whether you are reading an error or turning on maintenance mode.

"Can't I just build this myself?"​

You can, and many teams start that way: an environment variable here, a maintenance.html there, a flags table in the database. It works until it doesn't:

  • Changing an environment variable usually means a restart, and often a deploy.
  • Home-grown flags tend to be on or off for everyone. Gradual rollouts that keep each user in the same bucket, and allow-lists for your own team, take real work to get right.
  • None of it reaches the browser tab that is already open. That needs a client that polls for changes and knows how to show a maintenance screen, a banner or a reload prompt.
  • Nobody remembers it exists until the incident, and then nobody remembers how it works.

The value of a control room is not any single switch. It is that the switches are always there, always wired up, and everyone knows where they are.

Start small​

You do not need to adopt everything on day one. A good first step is a single kill switch: wrap your riskiest new feature in a flag, ship it switched off, and turn it on from the console. The first time you turn it off again in the middle of a problem, without opening your editor, you will understand why web apps need a control room.

Connect your first app, or read What is ACR? for the full tour.

item.title: What is ACR? A control room for every application you run
item.description: ACR puts observing a web app and changing how it behaves in one console. Here is what it does, how it works and what it deliberately is not.
item.content:encoded:
Most teams run production with two separate toolboxes. One tells you what is happening: analytics, an error tracker, a log viewer, maybe an uptime pinger. The other lets you change what happens: a deploy pipeline, a feature-flag service, a config file someone has to edit over SSH. When something goes wrong, you are the glue between them.

ACR (Application Control Room) puts both halves in one place. You observe what your apps are doing, and you change how they behave while they are running, from the same console, through the same SDK.

Two halves, one loop​

Observe​

Install an SDK and your app starts reporting:

  • Visitors and sessions, with pages, referrers, browsers, devices and countries, in Analytics.
  • Your own events, like checkout_started or invoice_paid, with attributes you can filter on, in Events.
  • Errors, grouped into issues with readable stack traces, in Errors.
  • Log lines with levels from debug to fatal, plus a live tail, in Logs.
  • Request timings and Core Web Vitals, with p50, p95 and p99, in Performance.
  • Server heartbeats: CPU, memory, event loop and garbage collection for each Node.js process.

Around that sit Uptime checks for your public URLs, PM2 process monitoring, Releases that track adoption and crash-free sessions per version, and Alerts that turn the signals you care about into incidents on email, Slack, Discord, Teams or a webhook.

Control​

This is the half most monitoring tools leave out. From Controls and Flags you can, without a deploy:

  • turn a feature flag on for your team, then 5%, then everyone, and off again in one click;
  • put the app into maintenance mode, with a message and a list of users who can still get in;
  • show an announcement banner to every visitor, now or on a schedule;
  • tell outdated tabs that a new version is available, or force them to reload;
  • clear stale caches and service workers in every open browser;
  • turn telemetry collection off entirely, sample it, or raise the minimum log level.

How it works​

Both halves travel over the same channel. The SDK batches telemetry and sends it to ACR. Separately, it polls one small, cached JSON document called the control snapshot, which holds everything you configured under Controls and Flags. SDKs check about once a minute and only download the snapshot when it changed.

That design has a few consequences you will feel right away:

  • No inbound ports. ACR never connects into your app. Your app always calls out, so there is nothing to expose or firewall.
  • Flags cost nothing to read. They are evaluated inside the SDK from the last snapshot, so checking a flag never makes a network request, and keeps working offline.
  • Changes land in about a minute, and immediately when a browser tab comes back into focus.

The rules ACR follows​

A few principles shape the whole product.

Everything belongs to an app. There are no workspaces, organizations or environments to configure. "Shop - production" and "Shop - staging" are two apps, each with its own keys, members and data. One app is one thing you deploy.

The credential decides the app. An SDK request never says which app it belongs to. ACR works that out from the API key, so nobody can write into another app by editing a payload. Browser keys only work from the origins you allow, and server secrets never go into a browser bundle; the browser SDK refuses them.

Telemetry must never hurt your app. SDK calls never throw. Buffers have a fixed size. Failed sends retry with backoff, and when ACR is busy it asks clients to slow down instead of falling over.

Privacy by default. Query strings are stripped, sensitive keys are redacted, email addresses in free text are masked, and visitor IP addresses are never stored.

What ACR is not (yet)​

Being clear about this saves you time:

  • It is not a distributed tracing backend. Trace and span ids travel with your logs and errors so you can filter by them, but ACR does not store traces or custom metrics.
  • It does not instrument every transport. HTTP is covered; GraphQL, WebSocket and microservice transports in NestJS are not instrumented automatically.
  • It is built for JavaScript first. There are SDKs for the browser, React, Angular, Node.js, Express and NestJS. Services in other languages can still send events through the public events API.

Who it is for​

ACR is for the people who ship a web app and then have to keep it healthy: small product teams without a dedicated operations group, developers who want to see their errors next to the switch that fixes them, and anyone who has ever wished they could turn a feature off faster than their deploy pipeline allows.

Try it​

Connect your first app takes a few minutes: create an app, add an API key, install an SDK and watch the first visitor arrive. Then open Controls, flip maintenance mode on, and watch your own app respond within a minute. That moment is the whole idea of ACR.
